RUMOAR®FILE 001
The thesis

I've found a consumer behaviour the market isn't organised around.

The market is organised around products. The consumer is organised around identity. Every accessory sits in a different aisle, under a different brand, in a different tab — while the man buying them is assembling one self.

THESIS02
The behaviour — click any stage

Demand is created upstream.
It breaks at step three.

01
See
A creator wears something. The consumer notices. Discovery has already left the retailer.
02
Save
He screenshots it. The moment of desire is captured — and stored somewhere no brand can see.
03
Search
The break. The Indian market often doesn't carry the product — or offers a cheaper copy instead.
04
Ask
"Where's this from?" He turns to comments, DMs and communities for an answer nobody owns.
05
Buy
Only if he can find it. Demand created upstream goes unfulfilled downstream.

PRICE ARCHITECTURE05
What customers actually write in reviews

“Design is not a nice-to-have.”

Design is the strongest positive theme in the category — ahead of price, ahead of capacity. Durability still rates highest when it shows up, but design is what gets mentioned unprompted. When consumers get it, they reward it.

ROADMAP09
The opportunity

Identity isn't one category.

How it works today

A complete look — bag, eyewear, cap, watch, jewellery, shoes — means six brands and six separate shopping journeys. The consumer assembles an identity on his own.

The RUMOAR model

One consumer, one identity, many products. We organise around the person, not the product — one destination for every accessory that makes up a man's look.

OPERATING MODEL14
Strategy

White-labeling is a feature.

Speed first

At the start, speed beats ownership. White-labeling lets us learn fast: which silhouette, fabric, colour, price point, occasion and identity resonates. Curation gives us velocity.

Winners go proprietary

Once we know what works, we own it. Proven products become proprietary lines — built on real signal, not guesswork. Proprietary product gives us defensibility.

STRATEGY15
Competitive advantage

Anyone can copy a bag.

The product can be copied. The taste engine is not.

Five moves, run continuously. The advantage compounds in the loop, not in any single SKU sitting inside it.

DEFENSIBILITY16

The consumer has already moved.

Consumer behaviour, already shifted
  1. Creators are becoming discovery
  2. Styling is becoming content
  3. Accessories are becoming identity products
  4. Indian D2C has proven men will pay for design

The market is still stuck in 2015.

The gap no one has closed
  1. Accessories are distributed, priced and packaged like commodity goods
  2. No brand owns the premium men's accessory space in India
  3. Demand is present — the supply side has not caught up

That lag is the window. Consumer intent is ahead of the market by years.

TIMING17

Own a slice,
not the whole market.

The question isn't “can this market be big?” It's “can we take about 1% of the relevant one?” Bags, eyewear and headwear are large existing consumer pools. Narrow to Indian men, 22–35, design-conscious and digitally discoverable, and the opportunity is clear and winnable.

MARKET18
The business model — drag the wheel

Betting on assortment, not one hero SKU.

More designs create more reasons to discover, buy and come back. Content feeds discovery, discovery feeds product, purchase feeds data, data feeds curation — and curation makes the next design better than the last.
